_notice: FICTITIOUS. Brennick syndrome, the IBSC, the Brennick Functional Scale and every figure here are invented. Nothing here describes a real disease.
usage: Approved unbranded disease statements. Either bot may use them: the HCP bot uses text, the patient-services assistant uses patient_text. They carry no product information, and the validator rejects any mention of the product, its ingredients, the predecessor or the support program. A disease statement must never be merged with a product claim into a sentence that implies the product addresses it (for example, pairing DIS-011 with an efficacy claim to suggest QUORVANTA prevents progression).

facts.text: Brennick syndrome (BrS) is a chronic, immune-mediated disorder of the central nervous system characterized by inflammation around small blood vessels in the brainstem and spinal cord, with damage to nearby nerve fibers.
facts.patient_text: Brennick syndrome is a long-term condition in which the immune system causes inflammation in the brainstem and spinal cord, which can damage nerve fibers.

facts.text: An estimated 410,000 adults in the United States were living with BrS in 2021.
facts.patient_text: About 410,000 adults in the United States live with Brennick syndrome.

facts.text: BrS is diagnosed about 2.5 times as often in women as in men, and symptoms most often begin between the ages of 20 and 45.
facts.patient_text: Brennick syndrome is more common in women, and it usually starts between the ages of 20 and 45.

facts.text: Under the 2021 IBSC criteria the disease course is classified as first clinical episode, relapsing-remitting, active progressive, non-active progressive, or primary progressive.
facts.patient_text: Doctors describe Brennick syndrome by how it behaves over time: a first episode, relapsing-remitting, or one of several progressive forms.

facts.text: In a 30-year natural history registry, 82% of patients had a relapsing course at onset and 18% a primary progressive course.
facts.patient_text: Most people, about 8 in 10, start with a relapsing form of Brennick syndrome.

facts.text: A relapse is new or worsening neurological symptoms lasting at least 48 hours, in the absence of fever or infection, at least 30 days after the start of any previous relapse.
facts.patient_text: A relapse is when new symptoms appear, or old ones get worse, for at least 2 days, without a fever or infection to explain them.

facts.text: Untreated patients with relapsing-remitting BrS had between 0.3 and 0.5 relapses per year on average in the natural history registry.

Diagnosis under the 2021 IBSC criteria requires a typical clinical episode, MRI lesions in at least two of four characteristic regions (brainstem, cervical spinal cord, cerebellar peduncles, periaqueductal region), and exclusion of other causes; a positive cerebrospinal fluid BRK index may substitute for one MRI region.
facts.patient_text: Brennick syndrome is diagnosed using your symptoms, MRI scans, and sometimes a test of the fluid around the spinal cord, after other causes have been ruled out.

facts.text: On MRI, T2 lesions reflect areas of current or past inflammation, and contrast-enhancing (CE+) lesions indicate inflammation active within approximately the previous 6 weeks.
facts.patient_text: MRI scans show areas of inflammation. Some show recent activity and some show older changes.

facts.text: The Brennick Functional Scale (BFS) is a clinician-rated scale from 0 (normal neurological examination) to 8 (unable to walk), in whole-point steps, based on six functional domains and walking ability. BFS 4 corresponds to walking limited to about 500 meters without aid or rest, and BFS 6 to needing a walking aid to walk 100 meters.
facts.patient_text: Doctors use a scale called the Brennick Functional Scale, from 0 to 8, to measure how Brennick syndrome affects things like movement, balance, vision and walking.

facts.text: Confirmed disability progression is defined as an increase of at least 1 BFS point sustained for 12 weeks.
In the natural history registry, about half of untreated patients with relapsing-remitting BrS had developed a progressive course within 15 years of onset.
Fatigue was the most frequently reported symptom in the natural history registry, by about 70% of patients.
facts.patient_text: Tiredness (fatigue) is the most common symptom, reported by about 7 in 10 people with Brennick syndrome.

facts.text: Having a first-degree relative with BrS modestly increases risk; no single inherited cause has been identified.
facts.patient_text: Brennick syndrome isn't passed down in a simple way, although having a close relative with it slightly raises the chance of getting it.

facts.text: The goals of disease-modifying therapy in relapsing BrS are to reduce relapses and new MRI lesions and to slow disability progression. Therapies are available as oral, injectable and infused medicines, and the choice depends on disease activity, safety, monitoring and patient preference.
facts.patient_text: There are several kinds of long-term treatment for relapsing Brennick syndrome, including pills, injections and infusions. Your healthcare provider can talk with you about which may suit you.

facts.text: Short courses of high-dose corticosteroids are commonly used to speed recovery from a relapse; they do not change the long-term course of the disease.
